explicit_validation.explanation: Paper explicitly validates LLM-as-a-judge against human evaluation by comparing judgments on the same 1,000 samples and reports percentage agreement metrics

prompts.notes: Prompts available in Appendix sections 'Table : Instruction of fact extraction for hallucination detection' and 'Table 10: Instruction of fact verification for hallucination detection' with intention descriptions and in-context demonstrations

guidelines.notes: Human labelers annotated hallucination types using the taxonomy defined in Section 2 (Entity-error, Relation-error, Incompleteness, Outdatedness, Overclaim, Unverifiability), with each sample labeled by two labelers and examined by one checker

sample_size.notes: Based on semantic similarity score, selected 1,000 questions (200 per domain) from HaluEval 2.0 for validation

correlation_interpretation.threshold_used: Not explicitly stated, but described as 'high consistency'

validation_results.summary_finding: LLM-based detection method achieves 91.5-94.7% agreement with human annotation across five domains, demonstrating high reliability for hallucination detection

human_only_criteria: specific hallucination types (Entity-error, Relation-error, Incompleteness, Outdatedness, Overclaim, Unverifiability)
criteria_mapping.notes: LLM judges overall factuality/hallucination at statement level (True/False/Unknown), while human evaluators provide finer-grained annotation using the hallucination taxonomy
